# PART 1 - Diamonds

## Narrative

In this part, I will be exploring how the physical dimensions of diamonds length ($x$), width ($y$), and depth ($z$) vary across different color categories from D to J.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
#| include: false
#| warning: false

#load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

#load data
data(diamonds)

```

### Diamonds Tables of Statistics


```{r}
#| label: diamonds-prep
#| include: false

#DIAMONDS

# Filter out 0 values 
clean_diamonds <- diamonds |>
  filter(x > 0 & y > 0 & z > 0)

# Table for Length (x)
table_x <- clean_diamonds |>
  group_by(color) |>    # group diamonds by their color
  summarise(      # summarizing all descriptive statistics
    count = n(),
    Min = min(x),
    Q1 = quantile(x, .20),
    Q2 = quantile(x, .40),
    Median = median(x),
    Q3 = quantile(x, .60),
    Q4 = quantile(x, .80),
    Max = max(x),
    Mean = mean(x),
    SD = sd(x)
  )

# Table for Width (y)
table_y <- clean_diamonds |>
  group_by(color) |>
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    Min = min(y),
    Q1 = quantile(y, .20),
    Q2 = quantile(y, .40),
    Median = median(y),
    Q3 = quantile(y, .60),
    Q4 = quantile(y, .80),
    Max = max(y),
    Mean = mean(y),
    SD = sd(y)
  )

# Table for Depth (z)
table_z <- clean_diamonds |>
  group_by(color) |>
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    Min = min(z),
    Q1 = quantile(z, .20),
    Q2 = quantile(z, .40),
    Median = median(z),
    Q3 = quantile(z, .60),
    Q4 = quantile(z, .80),
    Max = max(z),
    Mean = mean(z),
    SD = sd(z)
  )
```

**Diamond Length (x) Statistics by Color**

@tbl-length shows a statistics table titled “Descriptive Statistics of Diamond Length (x) by Color” which lists seven diamond color categories, D through J, across 11 columns: color, count, Min, Q1, Q2, Median, Q3, Q4, Max, Mean, and SD. The table has thin horizontal rules and alternating light-gray row shading. Counts range from 2,808 for J to 11,284 for G; the listed means range from 5.41 for E to 6.52 for J.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-length
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive Statistics of Diamond Length (x) by Color"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

#diamond(x)

knitr::kable(table_x, digits = 2) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"))

```

# PART 2 - BIG10

## Narrative

In this part, I will be examining the relationship between offensive and defensive performance across teams using the `team_box.csv` dataset.

```{r}
#| label: btaa-prep
#| include: false

#BIG!0 BTAA LOVE

team_box <- read_csv("team_box.csv") #reading csv

team_stats <- team_box |>
  group_by(team_id) |> #grouping by teams
  summarise( #finding average score & opp score
    avg_score = mean(team_score, na.rm = TRUE), 
    avg_opp_score = mean(opponent_team_score, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

```

@fig-team-stats shows a scatter plot titled “Average Points Scored vs Allowed Per Game” which shows average points scored on the horizontal axis and average points allowed on the vertical axis. Blue, semi-transparent circular points form a broad downward-sloping pattern: higher scoring values generally align with fewer points allowed. The densest cluster is around 60–70 points scored and 60–70 allowed; a more dispersed group spans roughly 30–60 scored and 70–110 allowed. A few points lie well above or to the right of the main clusters.

```{r}
#| label: fig-team-stats
#| fig-cap: "Average Points Scored vs Allowed Per Game"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-pos: "H"

#BIG10 avg score vs avg allowed

team_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_score, y = avg_opp_score)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "blue", size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Points Scored vs Allowed Per Game",
    x = "Average Points Scored",
    y = "Average Points Allowed"
  )

```



# PART 3 - Monte Carlo

## Narrative 

In this part, I will be running a Monte Carlo simulation to estimate the area under a chi-square curve. I tested four different sample sizes ($n = 10$, $100$, $1,000$, and $10,000$).


```{r}
#| label: mc-prep
#| include: false


mc_simulation <- function(n) {  #running simulation
  x_vals <- runif(n, min = 0, max = 20)
  y_vals <- runif(n, min = 0, max = 0.16)
  
  sim_data <- data.frame(x = x_vals, y = y_vals) |>
    mutate(
      curve_val = dchisq(x, df = 5),
      flag = ifelse(y <= curve_val, "on/below", "above")
    )
  return(sim_data)
}

rect_area <- 20 * 0.16    # setting rectangle area

make_mc_plot <- function(n_pts) {  #creation of plots
  sim_df <- mc_simulation(n_pts)
  onBelow <- mean(sim_df$flag == "on/below")
  integral_est <- rect_area * onBelow
  
  ggplot(sim_df, aes(x = x, y = y, color = flag)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("above" = "red", "on/below" = "green")) +
    stat_function(
      fun = dchisq,
      args = list(df = 5),
      xlim = c(0,20)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste("n =", n_pts),
      subtitle = paste("Est. Int:", round(integral_est, 4)),
      x = "x",
      y = "y"
    ) +
    theme(legend.position = "none") 
}
# making individual plots for sizes of n
plot10 <- make_mc_plot(10)
plot100 <- make_mc_plot(100)
plot1000 <- make_mc_plot(1000)
plot10000 <- make_mc_plot(10000)

#plots put together
mc_grid <- (plot10 + plot100) / (plot1000 + plot10000)

```

@fig-mc-grid shows four Monte Carlo integration plots arranged in a two-by-two grid. Each has gray gridlines, x and y axes, red points labeled “above,” and a green curve labeled “on/below.” The green curve rises sharply near x = 0, peaks around y = 0.15, then declines toward zero by x = 20. From upper left to lower right, the plots show increasingly dense red and green points around the curve. The displayed estimated integrals are 0.64, 0.928, 1.0656, and 0.9824.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mc-grid
#| fig-cap: "Monte Carlo Integration Convergence Across Sample Sizes (n = 10 to 10,000)"
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
#| warning: false
#| fig-pos: "H"

mc_grid

```



# PART 4 - Calcium

## Narrative

In this part, I will be tidying the `calcium.csv` dataset to track how average ulnar calcium changes over four years between the Null group and the Diet/Exercise group. After outlining a step by step data wrangling plan, I will compare the visualizations generated by ChatGPT when given my detailed plan versus when given a generic prompt.


## Creating a Plan

**Goal:** Clean up the `calcium.csv` dataset so each row is one measurement for one woman at one point in time, and create a line graph showing how average ulnar calcium changes over four years for the Null group (15 women) compared to the Diet/Exercise group (16 women).

**Needs:**
* **Data:** The original `calcium.csv` file
* **Software:** The `tidyverse` package to reshape the data and make the graph.

**Steps:**

1. **Separate the Two Groups:**
   * Load `calcium.csv` into Rstudio
   * Split the table in half: columns 1–4 for the Null group, and columns 5–8 for the Diet/Exercise group.
   * Remove the blank 16th row from the Null group so it only has 15 women, while the Diet/Exercise group has all 16.

2. **Label the Women and Time Points:**
   * Give each of the 31 women an ID number
   * Add a `Group` column labeled `"Null"` for the 15 women in the first group, and `"Diet/Exercise"` for the 16 women in the second group.
   * Make sure the four time columns in both groups are clearly named `Initial`, `Year 1`, `Year 2`, and `Year 3`.

3. **Stack into Tidy Format:**
   * Stack the two groups back together and combine the four year columns into two columns: `Year` and `Calcium`.
   * Make sure the final table has 124 rows (31 women $\times$ 4 years) and 4 columns (`ID`, `Group`, `Year`, `Calcium`).

4. **Make the Graph:**
   * Create a line plot with `Year` on the x axis and `Calcium` on the y axis, colored by `Group`.
   * Plot one bold line showing the average trend for each group over the four years.
   * Add a clear title and axis labels so the difference between the two groups is easy to see.
   
   
## CHATGPT using plan to create data visualization


![Average Ulnar Calcium Over Four Years by Group (chatgpt plan output)](chatgpt_graph.png){#fig-chatgpt-plan width=85% fig-pos="H"}


## CHATGPT creating a data visualization with a generic prompt


![Mean Values across all 8 columns (chatgpt generic output)](chatgpt_generic_graph.png){#fig-chatgpt-generic width=85% fig-pos="H"}

## Narrative: Compare and Contrast CHATGPT Outputs

Both of the visualizations are built in CHATGPT-6 from the same calcium dataset, so they reflect the same underlying pattern where values peak early and then drop towards the final time point. However, giving CHATGPT a plan made the final graph clearer and easier to read. Without the plan, CHATGPT treated the columns as eight separate bars with basic labels like Set 1 y0, Set 2 y2, which made it hard to compare the two groups over time. With the plan, ChatGPT properly organized the data into the Null and Diet/Exercise groups across the four years and used a line graph, making the group trends stand out clearly.
